title: Writing Melodies
intro: A melody people remember usually has a clear shape, a comfortable range, a short idea that returns, and a rhythm that fits the words. These are tendencies, not rules, but they are where most strong tunes start.

blocks.text: The overall shape of a melody, its contour, is what listeners remember first. Common shapes are the arch (rise to a high point, fall back), the descent from a high start, and the wave. A melody that stays on one note sounds like a chant; one that leaps everywhere is hard to sing. A good balance is mostly steps with occasional leaps, each larger leap followed by a step back the other way (the same 'gap-fill' habit that counterpoint teaches, see Counterpoint (#/arts/music-theory/counterpoint)).

Most popular melodies sit within about an octave to a tenth. Save the highest note for the most important moment, usually in the chorus, and reach it only once or twice; a high point that keeps coming back loses its effect. Writing at the piano, sing everything you play: if you cannot sing it comfortably, a singer will not either.

Strong melodies are built from a short idea, a motive, repeated and varied: the same rhythm on new pitches (a sequence), the same shape answered by a contrasting one, an idea extended at the end of a phrase. Listeners enjoy predicting what comes next and being slightly surprised (Huron's Sweet Anticipation explains why). Repeat enough to be learned, vary enough to stay interesting.

blocks.text: On strong beats and long notes, melodies mostly use chord tones (root, 3rd, 5th of the chord underneath); on weak beats they move through passing and neighbour tones (see Non-Chord Tones (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/non-chord-tones)). The 3rd of the chord is the most expressive melody note; the root is the most stable and works as an ending. A non-chord tone held on a strong beat, an appoggiatura or suspension, is the most emotional move a melody can make: lean on it and resolve it.

Melodic rhythm should follow the natural rhythm of the words: stressed syllables on strong beats or long notes ('to-DAY', not 'TO-day'). Contrast between sections often comes from rhythm alone: busy, syncopated verses and longer, simpler chorus notes, or the reverse.

A hook is the short, catchy part listeners remember, usually the title in the chorus. It tends to be short (two bars or less), rhythmically distinctive, repeated several times, and placed on the highest or most stable notes of the song. Instrumental hooks (a riff, a synth line) work the same way.

items: Write a four-bar melody over a single held chord using only chord tones on beats 1 and 3, then add passing tones between them.
Take a motive of three or four notes and write three variations: in sequence, inverted, and with the rhythm changed.
Sing a melody over four chords you like, record it, then trim it to its strongest two bars.

blocks.title: Chord tones
blocks.text: Over a G major chord on beat 1, which of these melody notes are chord tones: G, A, B, C, D?
solution: G major is G–B–D. So G, B and D are chord tones; A and C are not (they could be passing or neighbour tones).

blocks.text: Sources: Perricone, J. (2018). Great Songwriting Techniques. Oxford University Press; Webb, J. (1998). Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting. Hyperion; Huron, D. (2006). Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation. MIT Press; Zollo, P. (2003). Songwriters on Songwriting, revised ed. Da Capo.
